title: USCIS Starts Approving H-1B Petitions Without $100,000 Fee After Stall
excerpt: Petitions for workers abroad that sat past their premium-processing deadlines for weeks are now being approved with no $100,000 payment, as two federal court orders blocking the fee hold firm.
body:
• USCIS has started approving H-1B petitions for workers outside the United States without collecting the $100,000 fee, after weeks in which premium-processing cases sat past their 15-business-day deadline with no decision.
  • Two federal courts are blocking the fee: a Massachusetts court vacated it nationwide in June 2026, and a Northern District of California court barred enforcement again in late September 2026, including under the extension through September 21, 2027.
  • For readers: if your employer filed a fee-subject petition between June and August 2026 under premium processing and it is still pending past 15 business days, attorneys say it may need a direct push — approvals are moving unevenly, not all at once.
  • The relief is not final: the government has appealed in both the First and Ninth Circuits and USCIS says it will collect the fee if the court orders are lifted, so employers are being urged to act on approvals quickly.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has started approving H-1B petitions that would have been subject to President Donald Trump's $100,000 fee even though the employers never paid it, according to immigration law firms tracking the cases. The approvals end a stall in which petitions for workers outside the United States sat untouched for weeks, well past the 15-business-day window USCIS guarantees for premium processing.

The shift matters most for the petitions filed between June and August 2026. Attorneys at Harris Beach Murtha report that those cases, filed under premium processing for beneficiaries abroad, are now being adjudicated without any requirement to pay the $100,000. Meltzer Hellrung, which had organized a multi-company mandamus action to compel USCIS to decide the stalled cases, says approvals began coming through after the firm publicized the logjam, without a lawsuit ever being filed.

How the fee was blocked

The fee began with a September 2025 presidential proclamation that imposed a $100,000 payment on certain new H-1B petitions, chiefly those for workers outside the United States who would need consular processing. Petitions seeking a change of status or extension for workers already in the United States were not covered. On September 18, 2026, the president extended the restriction through September 21, 2027.

https://x.com/LEBcando/status/2113985421097013290

Two courts then blocked it. In June 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the fee nationwide, finding the executive branch lacked authority to impose it. The government appealed, but in July the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit declined to keep the fee in effect while the appeal proceeds. At the end of September 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California also barred enforcement, finding the government had failed to follow required rulemaking procedures — a second, independent block that also covers the September 2026 extension. The government has appealed that ruling to the Ninth Circuit.

"The Court finds that the Policy imposes a tax on H-1B petitions without the requisite delegation by Congress."

— U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin, Massachusetts ruling vacating the fee

USCIS has said it is complying with the orders, but that it will collect the fee if they are lifted. The full status picture is tracked in the Harris Beach Murtha status update and in Meltzer Hellrung's account of the approvals now being issued without the fee.

Why cases stalled even after the courts ruled

The court orders did not immediately unblock the pipeline. Despite the vacatur, attorneys nationwide reported that H-1B petitions for workers abroad were effectively placed on indefinite hold for several weeks, even under premium processing. Only in October 2026 did adjudications visibly resume. Approvals remain uneven — not every stalled petition is moving at the same pace, and a case still sitting past its premium processing deadline may need direct follow-up through counsel.

What this means for Indian professionals and their employers

Indian nationals receive the largest share of H-1B visas each year, so the stall and its easing fall disproportionately on Indian engineers, physicians, researchers and the U.S. employers — from technology firms to universities and hospitals — trying to bring them in. Recruiters who had screened out candidates abroad because those petitions carried the $100,000 exposure now have reason to revisit those files. The fastest hires, attorneys note, may be candidates abroad who already hold a valid, unexpired H-1B visa stamp and were previously counted against the cap: in many cases they can travel on that visa with the new employer's approval notice, skipping both a new lottery and a long consular interview wait. The worker still cannot start until the petition is approved, and employers should confirm the stamp is unexpired and the candidate has no prior status issues before extending an offer.

What to watch next

Both appeals remain pending, and the outcome in the First or Ninth Circuit could restore the fee. A separate proposal would go further: DHS has proposed a $103,265 fee that would apply to all cap-subject petitions, including change-of-status filings for F-1 graduates — a broader reach than the original proclamation. That proposal is still in rulemaking and is not in effect. For now, the practical advice from both firms is the same: check every pending fee-subject petition, move quickly on approvals to schedule visa appointments or travel while the court orders stand, and keep contingency plans in case an appeals court revives the charge.
